pages.text: A blast furnace does not make steel. Coke burning in a hot blast reduces the ore as it sinks down the stack, and the iron melts, and iron that melts against coke dissolves carbon: three and a half to four and a half per cent of it, and silicon from the ash.
pages.title: Pig iron

pages.text: What runs out of the hearth is pig iron, named for the sand beds it was cast in, a sow feeding a row of pigs. It is hard and brittle and cannot be forged.

Crushed iron ore and a limesand in The Factory Must Grow's blast furnace give 216 mB of molten pig iron, 144 mB of molten slag and furnace gas; a raw iron lump, twice as much. That is half as much iron again as a bloomery gets from the same ore.

A bloomery never melts its iron and loses much of it to the slag as iron oxide; the blast furnace's lime slag carries almost none, and nearly all the iron goes into the pig (Tylecote, A History of Metallurgy).

Pig iron goes three ways: cast as it is, puddled to wrought iron, or blown to steel. Sources: Tylecote, A History of Metallurgy (2nd ed., 1992); Gale, Iron and Steel (1969); Ullmann's Encyclopedia of Industrial Chemistry, "Iron" and "Steel".
pages.title: Three ways
